endorsements.quote: Patients, in turn, require basic AI literacy.
Clinicians should check clinically consequential claims against the medical record, current clinical findings, guideline-based care, and professional judgment.

For moderate-risk or high-risk advice, including safety-critical items, minimum documentation should capture the clinically relevant AI-generated claim or recommendation, the reason for accepting, modifying, or rejecting it, any patient preference that materially affected the decision, and the final shared plan.
Clinicians should also recognize automation bias in patients and use concise, nonconfrontational strategies to restore epistemic balance without undermining patient agency [ 17 19 20 ].

Health systems may reduce inequity through standardized previsit symptom forms, nonproprietary patient-reported outcome tools, interpreter-accessible digital supports, and staff-assisted intake, helping prevent PH-LLM use from becoming an informal gateway to more attentive care.

unlisted_practices: Developers and platforms should disclose model identity and version, data sources, temporal anchoring, and uncertainty signals for clinically consequential PH-LLM outputs.

Health systems should require provenance disclosure, evidence links, audit logs, and data-source labeling as conditions for procurement, EHR integration, preferred app lists, or partnerships with commercial PH-LLM vendors.
Health systems should adopt a risk-stratified intake process categorizing patient-brought AI advice as low-risk, moderate to high risk, or safety-critical.
Safety-critical AI-generated alerts should trigger immediate clinical escalation through established institutional pathways.
Clinicians should treat PH-LLM output as patient-reported contextual information rather than verifiable clinical evidence when provenance is unavailable.
Health systems should keep triage grounded in clinical acuity and patient need rather than the presence of an AI-generated summary.
Health systems should establish documentation standards, escalation pathways, audit mechanisms, and adverse-event review processes for AI-influenced clinical decisions.
Health systems should train clinicians in AI-related clinical communication competence to redirect AI-versus-clinician disagreement toward evidence quality, risk, and patient values.

Health systems should apply data minimization, tiered consent, deletion controls, and restrictions on secondary use, advertising, or model training for sensitive PH-LLM data such as mental health disclosures.
Fairness monitoring of PH-LLMs should avoid routine collection of protected-attribute data, separate such data from interaction content, and analyze it in aggregate under access controls.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/commentary proposing a 3-layer clinical governance framework for patient-brought personal health LLM narratives into clinical encounters.
